title: Application Security: SecurityContexts and Capabilities

toc.title: Why a container should not be root
The Pod Security Standards and the securityContext

html:
1Why a container should not be root

A container is a process on the node. If it runs as root, with extra Linux capabilities and a writable file system, a bug in the app (or a stolen shell) has a lot of power. A securityContext shrinks that power. It exists at two levels:

Level Where Applies to
Pod spec.securityContext every container and some volumes
Container spec.containers[].securityContext that container; overrides the Pod setting for the same field

2The fields to know

Field Level Meaning
runAsUser, runAsGroup Pod, container the numeric user and group ID of the process
runAsNonRoot: true Pod, container refuse to start if the image would run as root (UID 0)
fsGroup Pod volumes are made group-owned by this GID (and the group is added to the process)
supplementalGroups Pod extra group IDs for the process
seccompProfile: {type: RuntimeDefault} Pod, container filter system calls with the runtime's default profile
allowPrivilegeEscalation: false container the process cannot gain more privileges than its parent (blocks setuid tricks)
readOnlyRootFilesystem: true container the image's file system cannot be written
privileged: true container almost all capabilities and host devices: avoid
capabilities.add / capabilities.drop container Linux capabilities (see below)
seLinuxOptions, appArmorProfile Pod, container mandatory access control profiles (platform specific) 
spec:
  securityContext:                 # Pod level
    runAsNonRoot: true
    runAsUser: 10001
    fsGroup: 2000
    seccompProfile: {type: RuntimeDefault}
  containers:
  - name: main
    image: busybox:1.36
    securityContext:               # container level
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
      readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
      capabilities:
        drop: ["ALL"]
        add: ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"]

Check what a container really runs as: k exec <pod> -- id. With runAsUser: 1000, runAsGroup: 3000, fsGroup: 2000 you see uid=1000 gid=3000 groups=2000,3000.

runAsNonRoot

runAsNonRoot: true does not choose a user: it only refuses to start a container that would be root. If the image's user is root or a name (not a number), the Pod fails with CreateContainerConfigError and the message container has runAsNonRoot and image will run as root. Fix it by adding a numeric runAsUser (not 0) or by using an image built for a non-root user. kubectl describe pod shows the message.

Read-only root file system

With readOnlyRootFilesystem: true a write to the image file system fails (Read-only file system). Apps that need scratch space get it from an emptyDir mounted at /tmp (or wherever they write). This is the standard hardening step and works well with nginx-type apps once you mount their cache and run directories.

fsGroup and volumes

A volume is often owned by root, so a non-root process cannot write to it. fsGroup: 2000 makes the kubelet change the group of the volume to 2000 and add 2000 to the process: files and directories become group-writable, and a non-root user in that group can write. Check with k exec <pod> -- stat -c %g /data.

3Linux capabilities

Root's power is split into about forty capabilities. A container starts with a default set (for example CHOWN, NET_BIND_SERVICE, SETUID, KILL). Give it only what it needs:

Capability Allows
NET_BIND_SERVICE bind a port below 1024
NET_ADMIN change network configuration (interfaces, routes, firewall)
SYS_TIME set the system clock
SYS_ADMIN a huge set; almost like root: avoid
CHOWN, SETUID, SETGID, KILL, DAC_OVERRIDE part of the default set

The pattern is drop everything, add back what you need:

capabilities:
  drop: ["ALL"]
  add: ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"]

Inside a container: grep Cap /proc/1/status. For a container with only NET_BIND_SERVICE, CapEff is 0000000000000400.

4The Pod Security Standards and the securityContext

Module 11 showed the Pod Security Admission labels. The restricted level requires, for every container, roughly this securityContext:

Requirement of restricted Setting
run as non-root runAsNonRoot: true (and a numeric runAsUser the image can use)
no privilege escalation allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
drop all capabilities (only NET_BIND_SERVICE may be added) capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]
a seccomp profile seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault (or Localhost)
no privileged containers, no host namespaces, no host paths do not set privileged, hostNetwork, hostPID, hostPath

baseline forbids privileged containers, host namespaces, host paths and added capabilities beyond a small set, but does not require non-root. When a manifest is rejected with violates PodSecurity "restricted:latest", the message lists each missing setting: fix them one by one.

Exam tip

. Pod-level fields (runAsUser, fsGroup, seccompProfile) go in spec.securityContext; container-level fields (allowPrivilegeEscalation, capabilities, readOnlyRootFilesystem, privileged) go in the container's securityContext. Putting a field at the wrong level is rejected by the API server (unknown field): use k explain pod.spec.securityContext and k explain pod.spec.containers.securityContext.

Exam tip

. A Pod's securityContext cannot be edited in place. Export the YAML, change it, delete and recreate the Pod (or edit the Deployment).

5Lab tasks

<!-- LABS: m12 -->

Lab 12.1: run as user group

Domain: Environment | Points: 6 | Time: about 6 minutes | Status: executed and validated on Kubernetes v1.37.0 (id m12-01-run-as-user-group)

Context: kubectl config use-context kind-ckad

In the namespace sc, create a Pod named secure (image busybox:1.36, command sleep 3600) whose processes run with the user ID 1000 and the group ID 3000. Wait until it is Running.

Reference solution (try the task first; on the exam ssh <node> replaces the lab's docker exec):

kubectl -n sc apply -f - <<'Y'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: secure}
spec:
  securityContext:
    runAsUser: 1000
    runAsGroup: 3000
  containers:
  - name: main
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep", "3600"]
Y
kubectl -n sc wait --for=condition=Ready pod/secure --timeout=120s
kubectl -n sc exec secure -- id

Lab 12.2: readonly rootfs

Domain: Environment | Points: 7 | Time: about 7 minutes | Status: executed and validated on Kubernetes v1.37.0 (id m12-02-readonly-rootfs)

Context: kubectl config use-context kind-ckad

In the namespace sc, create a Pod named locked (image busybox:1.36, command sleep 3600) whose container has a read-only root file system, but can still write to /tmp (give it a writable ephemeral volume mounted at /tmp). Wait until it is Running.

Reference solution (try the task first; on the exam ssh <node> replaces the lab's docker exec):

kubectl -n sc apply -f - <<'Y'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: locked}
spec:
  containers:
  - name: main
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep", "3600"]
    securityContext:
      readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
    volumeMounts:
    - {name: tmp, mountPath: /tmp}
  volumes:
  - name: tmp
    emptyDir: {}
Y
kubectl -n sc wait --for=condition=Ready pod/locked --timeout=120s
kubectl -n sc exec locked -- sh -c 'touch /etc/x || echo "root file system is read-only"; touch /tmp/ok && echo "tmp is writable"'

Lab 12.3: capabilities

Domain: Environment | Points: 7 | Time: about 7 minutes | Status: executed and validated on Kubernetes v1.37.0 (id m12-03-capabilities)

Context: kubectl config use-context kind-ckad

In the namespace sc, create a Pod named netcap (image busybox:1.36, command sleep 3600) whose container drops all Linux capabilities and adds back only NET_BIND_SERVICE. Wait until it is Running.

Reference solution (try the task first; on the exam ssh <node> replaces the lab's docker exec):

kubectl -n sc apply -f - <<'Y'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: netcap}
spec:
  containers:
  - name: main
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep", "3600"]
    securityContext:
      capabilities:
        drop: ["ALL"]
        add: ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"]
Y
kubectl -n sc wait --for=condition=Ready pod/netcap --timeout=120s
kubectl -n sc exec netcap -- grep CapEff /proc/1/status

Lab 12.4: restricted namespace

Domain: Environment | Points: 8 | Time: about 9 minutes | Status: executed and validated on Kubernetes v1.37.0 (id m12-04-restricted-namespace)

Context: kubectl config use-context kind-ckad

The namespace locked enforces the restricted Pod Security Standard. The manifest ~/work/strict.yaml (the Pod strict) is rejected. Fix the manifest so that the Pod is admitted and Running: keep the image busybox:1.36 and the command, and add what the standard requires (the container must run as a non-root user, must not allow privilege escalation, must drop all capabilities, and the Pod must use the RuntimeDefault seccomp profile).

Reference solution (try the task first; on the exam ssh <node> replaces the lab's docker exec):

kubectl apply -f ~/work/strict.yaml 2>&1 | head -5
cat > ~/work/strict.yaml <<'Y'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: strict
  namespace: locked
spec:
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true
    runAsUser: 10001
    seccompProfile: {type: RuntimeDefault}
  containers:
  - name: main
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep", "3600"]
    securityContext:
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
      capabilities:
        drop: ["ALL"]
Y
kubectl apply -f ~/work/strict.yaml
kubectl -n locked wait --for=condition=Ready pod/strict --timeout=120s

Lab 12.5: fsgroup volume

Domain: Environment | Points: 6 | Time: about 7 minutes | Status: executed and validated on Kubernetes v1.37.0 (id m12-05-fsgroup-volume)

Context: kubectl config use-context kind-ckad

In the namespace sc, create a Pod named shared (image busybox:1.36, command sleep 3600) that runs as user 1000, with the supplemental group 2000 applied to its volumes (fsGroup). It mounts an emptyDir volume data at /data. The directory /data must be owned by the group 2000 and writable by the user 1000.

Reference solution (try the task first; on the exam ssh <node> replaces the lab's docker exec):

kubectl -n sc apply -f - <<'Y'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: shared}
spec:
  securityContext:
    runAsUser: 1000
    fsGroup: 2000
  containers:
  - name: main
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep", "3600"]
    volumeMounts:
    - {name: data, mountPath: /data}
  volumes:
  - name: data
    emptyDir: {}
Y
kubectl -n sc wait --for=condition=Ready pod/shared --timeout=120s
kubectl -n sc exec shared -- sh -c 'ls -ld /data; touch /data/hello && echo writable'

Lab 12.6: fix runasnonroot

Domain: Environment | Points: 6 | Time: about 6 minutes | Status: executed and validated on Kubernetes v1.37.0 (id m12-06-fix-runasnonroot)

Context: kubectl config use-context kind-ckad

In the namespace sc, the Pod app is stuck in CreateContainerConfigError: it has runAsNonRoot: true, but its image would run as root. Fix it without removing runAsNonRoot and without changing the image: recreate the Pod from ~/work/app.yaml so that it runs as the non-root user 1000 and is Running.

Reference solution (try the task first; on the exam ssh <node> replaces the lab's docker exec):

kubectl -n sc describe pod app | grep -i "non-root"
kubectl -n sc delete pod app --wait=true
sed -i 's/^    runAsNonRoot: true/    runAsNonRoot: true\n    runAsUser: 1000/' ~/work/app.yaml
kubectl apply -f ~/work/app.yaml
kubectl -n sc wait --for=condition=Ready pod/app --timeout=120s

<!-- /LABS -->

6Recall questions

R1At which two levels can a securityContext be set, and which wins?

Show the answer

Pod level and container level; the container level wins for the same field.

R2What does runAsNonRoot: true do?

Show the answer

It makes the kubelet refuse to start a container that would run as root; it does not pick a user.

R3Why does a Pod with runAsNonRoot: true and a root image show CreateContainerConfigError?

Show the answer

The image would run as root; add a numeric runAsUser or use a non-root image.

R4What does fsGroup do?

Show the answer

It makes volumes group-owned by that GID and adds the group to the processes, so a non-root user can write.

R5How do you give a container only the capability to bind low ports?

Show the answer

capabilities: {drop: ["ALL"], add: ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"]}.

R6What does readOnlyRootFilesystem: true require from the app?

Show the answer

Writable paths must be separate volumes such as an emptyDir on /tmp.

R7What does allowPrivilegeEscalation: false stop?

Show the answer

A process gaining more privileges than its parent, for example through setuid binaries.

R8Which four settings does the restricted standard need on a typical container?

Show the answer

Non-root user, no privilege escalation, drop all capabilities and a seccomp profile (RuntimeDefault).

Quick Reference Card

Topic Remember
Levels Pod spec.securityContext, container securityContext (container wins)
Identity runAsUser, runAsGroup, runAsNonRoot, fsGroup
Hardening allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, readOnlyRootFilesystem: true, seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault
Capabilities drop: ["ALL"], then add only what is needed; NET_BIND_SERVICE
Restricted non-root, no escalation, drop ALL, seccomp
Verify exec <pod> -- id, stat -c %g /dir, grep CapEff /proc/1/status
Fields at wrong level use kubectl explain to see where they belong
